summary:
Lithuania sets no entry, visa or residence provisions specific to LGBT travellers. A trans visitor faces no question about gender identity at the border, and the immigration rules contain no LGBT-specific screening requirement.

The country has no working procedure for legal gender recognition. Article 5.1 of the Civil Code gives unmarried adults the right to change gender through medical intervention, but no implementing legislation has been enacted, so the right cannot be exercised through any administrative route. The Lithuanian Gay League in September 2025 described an 18-year gap between the statutory right and its implementation; an LGL item the previous month referred to 17 years of legal limbo. Both figures describe the same condition.

Two court actions in 2025 left the gap open. In August the Ukmergė Chamber of the Vilnius Regional District Court suspended a civil case on the amendment of civil-status gender documents and referred the question of the provisions' compliance with the Constitution to the Constitutional Court. In September the Constitutional Court declined to examine the referral, leaving the absence of legal provisions for changing gender markers and personal identification codes in official documents unaddressed.

Partner recognition has moved further than gender recognition. Marriage is reserved to opposite-sex couples by Article 38 of the 1992 Constitution and Article 3.12 of the Civil Code, and Article 3.229 had confined partnerships to heterosexual couples. On 17 April 2025 the Constitutional Court ruled that the absence of legal regulation of partnership institutions, including for same-sex couples, contradicts the Constitution, and granted same-sex couples the right to register partnerships through the courts until the Seimas passes a comprehensive registered-partnership law. In January 2019 that court held that foreign same-sex spouses must be granted residence permits, following the European Court of Justice's 2018 Coman ruling.

Protection against violence is on the statute book. Section 170(3) of the Criminal Code bans public instigation of violence against LGBT people. A 2010 preliminary investigation found that 160 of roughly 180 hate-speech instances, mostly online, concerned the LGBT community; perpetrators were usually fined and computers occasionally confiscated. ILGA-Europe's 2025 annual review records a systemic lack of targeted LGBTI hate-crime victim support.

Policing of assembly has been the sharper failure. In April 2024 the Seimas Ombudsperson found that police had failed to guarantee the LGBT community's right to peaceful assembly, citing an inadequate response to hostile provocateurs at an LGL assembly, and recommended measures to secure effective assembly rights. Earlier events show the pattern: the Vilnius City Council refused permission for a 2007 Pride on security grounds; Baltic Pride 2010 was halted by a court shortly before it began, reinstated one day prior, and then held under heavy policing with violence and 12 arrests; the 2013 march required litigation through every judicial instance before it could be held, drew about 500 participants and ended with 28 arrests including that of MP Petras Gražulis. Attendance has since grown, to around 10,000 at the 2019 Vilnius Pride and around 5,000 in 2023.

Expression rules aimed at minors have been used against public events and publications. A 16 June 2009 amendment to the Law on the Protection of Minors banned propaganda of homosexual, bisexual or polygamous relations for under-18s, and Parliament overrode President Adamkus's veto 87 to 6; Amnesty International called the amendment a huge step backwards at the time. On 22 December 2009 the anti-LGBT clauses were replaced by a broader ban on information promoting conceptions of marriage or family other than those in the Constitution. That provision restricted a Vilnius Pride 2013 advertisement to night-time broadcast with an adult-content logo, and in 2014 the Ministry of Culture age-labelled and then banned the children's book Gintarinė širdis because two stories involved same-sex relationships; the European Court of Human Rights Grand Chamber held in January 2023 that this violated Article 10. On 18 December 2024 the Constitutional Court struck the anti-LGBT provisions down as violating Article 25.

Article 39.1 of the Public Information Act, amended on 30 September 2010, briefly barred messages that depict or promote a sexual orientation. The wording was described as a translation error and removed on 16 June 2011, with sexual orientation added as a protected ground.
tangentialFactors:
The criminal law carries no prohibition on same-sex sexual activity. It has been legal since 1993, two years after the end of Soviet occupation, and had been criminal during the interwar period and under Soviet rule. The age of consent was equalised at 14 in 2003 to meet European Union accession criteria and raised to 16 on 2 July 2010 for all youth regardless of gender or sexual orientation.

Attempts to restrict expression have recurred without success at the legislative stage. Two bids to criminalise the public propagation of homosexual relations, carrying fines of 2,000 to 10,000 litas, were rejected by Parliament, unanimously in 2011 and again in 2013. In September 2013 Parliament was to consider five bills, among them a ban on gender reassignment on the premise that gender is determined genetically from the very moment of conception, a ban on adoption by same-sex couples, fines of up to 1,800 euros for organisers of events denigrating constitutional moral values, and a legalisation of anti-gay speech.

Accountability for official hostility has been uneven. The prosecution of former MP Petras Gražulis for anti-LGBTI ridicule was complicated by the immunity he held as a member of the European Parliament. In 2014 all major television stations refused to broadcast a pro-tolerance LGBT video clip over fears of breaching the Law on the Protection of Minors.

Partnership legislation has a long stalled history. A registered-partnership bill was preliminarily approved 46 to 17 in May 2017 and remained pending as of 2019, and in May 2021 more than 10,000 people protested against partnership legislation in Vilnius.
localsOnly:
Employment is a documented point of exposure for trans residents. Reporting in May 2025 recorded trans people in Lithuania describing open ridicule, isolation and psychological abuse at work, with experts characterising the labour market as systemically discriminatory.

The Office of the Equal Opportunities Ombudsperson published its second national review of the situation of transgender people in 2024, after a first in 2019, covering the legal framework, document changes, healthcare barriers, labour-market discrimination, data protection and public attitudes. It records the absence of a legal framework for trans rights and of any strategic approach to them.

Asylum processing has drawn criticism. ILGA-Europe's 2025 review records that LGBTI asylum seekers from Cameroon were granted protection only after a four-year wait, under dire camp conditions, and that a psychologist was convicted of coercing asylum seekers into sexual acts.

Adoption remains closed to same-sex couples because marriage is a prerequisite, and although single applicants are theoretically eligible, adoption by single gay people is in practice not legally possible. President Gitanas Nausėda said in September 2021 that he would do his best to block adoption demands from Kaunas Pride organisers.
outOfScopeNotes:
The outcome of the five bills placed before the Seimas in September 2013 is not established by the sources consulted; only their introduction is documented.

No current text of Article 3.229 of the Civil Code is given, so whether it remains in force alongside the April 2025 Constitutional Court ruling is unresolved. Whether the court-registration route for partnerships opened by that ruling is operating in practice, and how many couples have used it, is not sourced.

With no implementing legislation for Article 5.1 of the Civil Code and no intervention by the Constitutional Court in September 2025, there is no administrative route to change gender markers or personal identification codes; when one will be created is unresolved.

The hate-speech figures date from a 2010 preliminary investigation and have not been updated in these sources. Whether the Seimas Ombudsperson's 2024 recommendations on assembly policing were implemented is not sourced.
